title: Al-Khwarizmi and algebra
hook: the mathematician whose name gives us algorithm and whose book gives us algebra

segments.voice: Yesterday, paper from Samarkand, warraqun: a cheaper page, and suddenly more people could own a book. Your line was: paper changed everything. What did you write on paper yesterday, and who was it for? Day nine hundred seventeen.

A man has died and left his estate. Some land, some coins, a debt to settle, a bequest to a friend. His widow, his daughters and his mother are all waiting. The Qur'an names their shares in fractions, a part to this one and a part to that, and somebody has to turn those fractions into actual coins in actual hands, with nobody cheated. Now multiply that by the families of a whole city. In Baghdad, a scholar at the caliph's court wrote a short book to help with exactly this kind of problem. His name was Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi. And the strange word in his book's title ended up in schoolbooks everywhere.
screen: `AN ESTATE TO DIVIDE.` → `SHARES IN FRACTIONS.` → `A BOOK TO HELP.`

segments.voice: The book is usually called the short book on calculating by al-jabr and al-muqabala. In his opening, al-Khwarizmi says why he wrote it: for what people need every day, in inheritance and wills, in dividing property, in lawsuits and trade, in measuring land and digging canals. It is a practical book, full of worked examples. So what are al-jabr and al-muqabala? They are two moves. Al-jabr means restoring, setting right what is broken. When one side of a problem has something taken away, you restore it, adding the missing piece back to both sides so the problem is whole again. Al-muqabala means balancing, setting one thing opposite another. When the same kind of thing sits on both sides, you take it off both, and what remains is simpler and still fair. Restore, then balance, and the unknown comes into the open. The usual account is that Latin readers later kept al-jabr from the title, and it became our word algebra. And the author's own name, al-Khwarizmi, the man from Khwarazm, is traced by dictionaries to our word algorithm, a step-by-step method. Notice what the two moves share with a court of law, or a family dividing an inheritance. Whatever you do to one side, you do to the other. Nothing is gained by cheating one side of the scale. The Qur'an asks people to keep the measure and not to cut short the balance. This week we watched a dynasty fall, a young man escape and start again, a round city rise, and the House of Wisdom gather books on cheap new paper. Here is what grew there: a way of thinking that restores and balances.
screen: `A BOOK FOR EVERYDAY NEEDS.` · `AL-JABR: RESTORING.` · `AL-MUQABALA: BALANCING.` · `WHAT YOU DO TO ONE SIDE, DO TO THE OTHER.` · then, large: `RESTORING AND BALANCING.`

segments.voice: The practice: do a small sum by hand. Find a pen and any scrap of paper. Settle, and breathe. Write something simple with a missing number: something plus three makes ten. Now do the balancing move: take three from both sides, and keep the scale level. Write what's left. Then sit with the page for the rest of the time. Notice the steadiness of it: one side, the other side, kept equal. If you pray, you can begin with bismillah. If you don't, just breathe with the balance. The bell holds the time.
Al-Khwarizmi. The scholar in Baghdad's House of Wisdom whose book of al-jabr, restoring, and al-muqabala, balancing, gave us the word algebra. Today's word.

Your line: restoring and balancing. Today, when something feels lopsided, at work or at home, ask the two questions. What is missing that needs restoring? What sits on both sides and can be set down? Day nine hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: Muslim scholars working in Baghdad wrote practical mathematics for daily needs, and inheritance law, with its shares named in the Qur'an, was one of the problems their arithmetic served.

pairs: a problem his book was written for

myth: al-Khwarizmi wrote his book as a puzzle for scholars only
his opening says it is for everyday needs: inheritance, trade, lawsuits, land and canals.
setting right what was broken: adding back what one side lost, to both sides.
in his method you may change one side without the other
whatever you do to one side, you do to the other. that is the balance.

fork.setup: you're al-Khwarizmi. one side of your problem has something taken away from it. what do you do?
options: ignore the missing part and guess.
restore it, adding it back to both sides.
fork.reveal: that is al-jabr, restoring: add back what was taken, on both sides, and the problem is whole again.

original.note: Arabic: restoring, setting right. the usual account says Latin readers kept it as algebra.

trapdoor: what you thought: algebra is school math with letters.
what it means: a book of two fair moves, restoring and balancing, written for inheritance, trade and land.
what a scholar hears: al-jabr wa'l-muqabala in the title; dictionaries trace algebra to al-jabr and algorithm to the name al-Khwarizmi.
recall: the direction you face in prayer

Etymologies algebra < al-jabr and algorithm < al-Khwarizmi are attributed ('the usual account', 'traced by dictionaries') because the index hook requires them; confirm the wording is acceptable under the claims rule.
Al-Khwarizmi's preface list of uses (inheritance, legacies, partition, lawsuits, trade, measuring land, digging canals) is paraphrased from memory of the Rosen 1831 translation; confirm.
'At the caliph's court' and 'in Baghdad': the book's dedication to al-Ma'mun is commonly cited; confirm.
Qur'an 55:7–9 paraphrased; quote Pickthall if a Keeper confirms the exact wording.
Editor: hook no longer tells the listener what they learned in school; practice now names the step 'the balancing move' (subtracting from both sides is al-muqabala, not al-jabr).

Audit: hook heirs changed from 'widow, children and brothers' to 'widow, daughters and mother': brothers are excluded when there is a son, and only the latter three have shares the Qur'an names in fractions (4:11–12).
